Low temperature makes the model select the most probable tokens, producing deterministic and focused outputs that are consistent across similar queries. High temperature (A, C) would introduce randomness, potentially leading to inconsistent or less accurate responses. Temperature does affect output reliability, so D is incorrect.

questions.question: What does the top-p (nucleus sampling) parameter do?

options.A: Selects only the single most probable next token
options.B: Sets a cumulative probability threshold so the model samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds the threshold
options.C: Limits the total number of tokens in the response
options.D: Controls the model's training learning rate

questions.explanation: Top-p (nucleus sampling) defines a cumulative probability threshold. The model considers only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds the top-p value. For example, with top-p=0.9, the model samples from the top tokens that together account for 90% of the probability mass, dynamically adjusting the number of candidates based on the probability distribution. It is not greedy decoding (A), token limit (C), or a training parameter (D).

questions.question: How does top-k differ from top-p in controlling model output?

options.A: Top-k and top-p are the same parameter with different names
options.B: Top-k limits sampling to a fixed number of most probable tokens, while top-p dynamically adjusts the candidate set based on cumulative probability
options.C: Top-k controls output length while top-p controls output quality
options.D: Top-k is used during training while top-p is used during inference

questions.explanation: Top-k limits the model to sampling from exactly the k most probable next tokens (a fixed number regardless of their probabilities). Top-p dynamically determines the candidate set based on cumulative probability, so the number of candidates varies depending on the probability distribution. They are not the same (A), both control sampling diversity not length/quality specifically (C), and both are inference-time parameters (D).

questions.question: A creative writing application needs a foundation model to generate diverse and imaginative stories. Which combination of inference parameters is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Temperature 0.0, top-p 0.1, top-k 1
options.B: Temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, top-k 50
options.C: Temperature 0.0, top-p 1.0, top-k 1
options.D: The inference parameters have no effect on creative writing quality

questions.explanation: For creative writing that requires diversity and imagination, higher temperature (0.8), higher top-p (0.95), and higher top-k (50) are appropriate. These settings allow the model to explore a wider range of token choices, producing more creative and varied outputs. Very low settings (A, C) would produce repetitive, deterministic text unsuitable for creative writing. Parameters absolutely affect output characteristics (D is wrong).

questions.question: What is the 'max tokens' parameter in foundation model inference?

options.A: The maximum number of tokens the model was trained on
options.B: The upper limit on the number of tokens the model will generate in its response
options.C: The maximum number of tokens in the model's vocabulary
options.D: The maximum number of API calls allowed per minute

questions.explanation: The max tokens parameter sets the upper limit on the number of tokens the model will generate in a single response. Once this limit is reached, the model stops generating even if the response is not complete. This parameter directly affects response length, cost (since pricing is often per-token), and latency. It is not about training data size (A), vocabulary size (C), or API rate limits (D).

questions.question: What is a context window in the context of foundation models?

options.A: A visual display showing the model's internal representations
options.B: The total number of tokens (input plus output) that a model can process in a single request
options.C: The time window during which the model is available for requests
options.D: The physical window on the server rack where the model is deployed

questions.explanation: A context window refers to the maximum total number of tokens (including both input/prompt tokens and output/generated tokens) that a foundation model can process in a single request. Models have fixed context window sizes (e.g., 4K, 8K, 32K, 128K, 200K tokens). Exceeding the context window causes either truncation of input or errors. It is not a visual display (A), availability window (C), or physical hardware component (D).

questions.question: A developer is building a document analysis application where users submit 50-page reports for summarization. The foundation model has a context window of 4,096 tokens. What problem will they encounter?

options.A: The model will process the document faster due to its small size
options.B: The 50-page report will exceed the model's context window, causing the input to be truncated or the request to fail
options.C: The model will automatically summarize only the first page
options.D: The model's temperature will automatically adjust to handle longer documents

questions.explanation: A 50-page report likely contains far more than 4,096 tokens (a typical page contains 300-500 tokens, so 50 pages could be 15,000-25,000 tokens). This exceeds the 4,096-token context window, meaning the input will be truncated (losing important content) or the request will fail entirely. Solutions include using a model with a larger context window, implementing chunked summarization, or using map-reduce strategies. The model does not auto-adjust (C, D).

questions.question: What is a stop sequence in foundation model inference?

options.A: A sequence of model weights that stops the training process
options.B: A specified string that, when generated by the model, signals it to stop generating further tokens
options.C: A keyboard shortcut that stops the inference API
options.D: A sequence of failed API calls that triggers an alert

questions.explanation: A stop sequence is a string (or set of strings) specified as an inference parameter that tells the model to stop generating tokens when it produces that string. For example, setting a stop sequence of '\n\n' would cause the model to stop after generating a double newline. This is useful for controlling output structure and preventing unnecessary generation beyond the desired response. It is not related to training (A), keyboard controls (C), or API monitoring (D).

questions.question: A model configured with temperature 0.5, top-p 0.9, and top-k 40 is producing responses that are too repetitive. Which parameter adjustment would MOST likely increase output diversity?

options.A: Decrease temperature to 0.1
options.B: Increase temperature to 0.8 and/or increase top-p to 0.95
options.C: Decrease top-k to 5
options.D: Set max tokens to 1

questions.explanation: To increase output diversity when responses are too repetitive, increase temperature (which flattens the probability distribution, giving less probable tokens more chance) and/or increase top-p (which expands the candidate token set). Decreasing temperature (A) or top-k (C) would make outputs even more repetitive. Setting max tokens to 1 (D) would generate only a single token per response.

questions.question: When should prompt engineering be chosen as the primary optimization approach for a foundation model?

options.A: When the model needs to learn entirely new domain knowledge not in its training data
options.B: When the task can be accomplished by better instructing the model using its existing knowledge, and rapid iteration at minimal cost is desired
options.C: When thousands of labeled training examples are available and compute budget is unlimited
options.D: When the model needs to access real-time information from external databases

questions.explanation: Prompt engineering should be the first approach when the model already has the necessary knowledge from pre-training and the task can be improved through better instructions, examples, or formatting. It offers rapid iteration at minimal cost with no training required. If the model lacks domain knowledge (A), fine-tuning or RAG is needed. Abundant labeled data (C) suggests fine-tuning. Real-time external data access (D) requires RAG.

questions.question: When is RAG the MOST appropriate optimization approach?

options.A: When you want to change the model's writing style and tone
options.B: When the model needs access to private, proprietary, or frequently updated information that was not in its training data
options.C: When you need the model to perform basic arithmetic
options.D: When you want to reduce the model's parameter count

questions.explanation: RAG is most appropriate when the model needs access to information that is private (company-specific), proprietary (not publicly available), or frequently updated (changes too rapidly for retraining). RAG retrieves this information from external knowledge bases at query time, supplementing the model's built-in knowledge. Changing style/tone (A) is better addressed by fine-tuning. Basic arithmetic (C) is handled by the model itself. Reducing parameters (D) requires distillation or pruning.

questions.question: When is fine-tuning the MOST appropriate optimization approach for a foundation model?

options.A: When you need the model to access today's news articles
options.B: When you need the model to consistently adopt a specific behavior, style, format, or domain-specific reasoning pattern that cannot be achieved through prompting alone
options.C: When you want the quickest possible improvement with zero cost
options.D: When the model needs to look up customer account information in real time

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning is most appropriate when you need the model to deeply internalize specific behaviors, styles, formats, or reasoning patterns that are difficult to achieve through prompt engineering alone. This includes adapting the model's tone, teaching it consistent output formats, or embedding domain-specific reasoning. Real-time information access (A, D) requires RAG. Quickest and cheapest improvement (C) is prompt engineering.

questions.question: A company has a large knowledge base of internal policies that changes monthly. They want a foundation model to answer employee questions about these policies. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Fine-tune the model monthly on the updated policies
options.B: Implement RAG with a knowledge base that is updated monthly with the latest policies
options.C: Memorize all policies in the system prompt
options.D: Train a new foundation model from scratch each month

questions.explanation: RAG is ideal for this scenario because: (1) the information changes monthly, making frequent fine-tuning impractical; (2) the policies are proprietary internal data; (3) RAG allows the knowledge base to be updated without model retraining; and (4) RAG can provide source citations to specific policy documents. Monthly fine-tuning (A) is expensive and slow. System prompt memorization (C) is limited by context window size. Training from scratch (D) is completely impractical.

questions.question: Which strategy is MOST effective for reducing foundation model inference costs when many users ask similar questions?

options.A: Using a larger, more expensive model to answer faster
options.B: Implementing response caching to serve cached answers for common queries
options.C: Increasing the temperature to generate shorter responses
options.D: Disabling the model and using static FAQ pages

questions.explanation: Response caching stores the generated answers for common queries and serves them directly without invoking the model, eliminating inference costs for repeated questions. This is highly effective when many users ask similar questions. Larger models (A) increase cost. Temperature (C) affects randomness, not length directly. Disabling the model (D) eliminates functionality entirely.

questions.question: A startup wants to optimize their foundation model usage costs on AWS. They currently use on-demand pricing for a highly variable workload with unpredictable spikes. Which cost optimization strategy should they implement FIRST?

options.A: Switch to provisioned throughput immediately
options.B: Set appropriate max token limits, monitor usage patterns with CloudWatch, and implement caching for common queries before making pricing model changes
options.C: Train their own foundation model to avoid API costs
options.D: Switch to the most expensive model to reduce the number of API calls

questions.explanation: For a startup with variable, unpredictable workloads, the first cost optimization steps should be: (1) set appropriate max token limits to avoid paying for unnecessarily long responses, (2) monitor usage patterns with CloudWatch to understand the workload, (3) implement caching for frequently asked queries to reduce API calls. Only after understanding usage patterns should they consider pricing model changes. Provisioned throughput (A) is better for predictable workloads. Training a custom model (C) is extremely expensive. Using the most expensive model (D) increases costs.

questions.question: A company uses a foundation model for two tasks: simple FAQ responses and complex document analysis. The complex task represents only 10% of requests. What cost optimization strategy would be MOST effective?

options.A: Use the most powerful model for all requests to ensure quality
options.B: Use a smaller, cheaper model for the 90% FAQ requests and route only complex analysis requests to the larger model
options.C: Use the cheapest model for all requests regardless of quality
options.D: Process all requests in batch once per day

questions.explanation: Model routing based on task complexity is the most effective strategy here. By using a smaller, cheaper model for the 90% of simple FAQ requests and reserving the larger, more capable model for the 10% of complex analysis requests, the company significantly reduces costs while maintaining quality where it matters. Using the most powerful model for everything (A) wastes money on simple tasks. The cheapest model for everything (C) sacrifices quality on complex tasks. Batch processing (D) adds unacceptable delay.

questions.question: Which AWS tool should be used to monitor and analyze foundation model usage costs over time?

options.A: Amazon Inspector
options.B: AWS Cost Explorer
options.C: Amazon GuardDuty
options.D: AWS Shield

questions.explanation: AWS Cost Explorer is the appropriate tool for monitoring and analyzing AWS costs over time, including foundation model usage costs from Amazon Bedrock. It provides visualizations of cost trends, forecasting, and the ability to filter by service, usage type, and time period. Amazon Inspector (A) is for security vulnerability assessment. Amazon GuardDuty (C) is for threat detection. AWS Shield (D) is for DDoS protection.

questions.question: A team is deciding between RAG and fine-tuning for their use case. They need the model to answer questions about data that changes daily and must cite specific sources. Which approach should they choose?

options.A: Fine-tuning, because it produces higher quality outputs
options.B: RAG, because it can incorporate daily data updates and naturally supports source citation from retrieved documents
options.C: Neither; they should train a new model from scratch
options.D: Fine-tuning, because it is faster to set up than RAG

questions.explanation: RAG is the clear choice for this use case for two reasons: (1) the data changes daily, making fine-tuning impractical since it would require daily retraining; (2) RAG naturally supports source citation since the model can reference the specific retrieved documents used to generate the answer. RAG's knowledge base can be updated daily without any model retraining. Fine-tuning (A, D) cannot handle daily data changes or provide document-level citations easily.

questions.question: A company wants their foundation model to consistently output responses in a very specific JSON schema with particular field names and formatting. Prompt engineering has been inconsistent. What should they try next?

options.A: RAG with JSON documents in the knowledge base
options.B: Fine-tuning on examples that demonstrate the exact desired JSON output format
options.C: Increasing the model's context window
options.D: Using a different vector database

questions.explanation: When prompt engineering cannot consistently achieve a specific output format, fine-tuning is the appropriate next step. By training the model on many examples of inputs paired with the exact desired JSON schema outputs, the model internalizes the formatting requirements and produces consistent outputs. RAG (A) helps with knowledge, not formatting. Context window (C) is about input/output length, not format. Vector databases (D) are irrelevant to output formatting.

questions.question: What is the recommended order for trying optimization techniques when adapting a foundation model for a new use case?

options.A: Fine-tuning first, then RAG, then prompt engineering
options.B: Prompt engineering first, then RAG if external knowledge is needed, then fine-tuning if behavior customization is required
options.C: RAG first, then training from scratch, then prompt engineering
options.D: Training from scratch, then fine-tuning, then prompt engineering

questions.explanation: The recommended order is: (1) Start with prompt engineering as it is the fastest, cheapest, and easiest to iterate; (2) Add RAG if the model needs access to external, private, or frequently updated information; (3) Consider fine-tuning if the model needs to deeply learn new behaviors, styles, or patterns that prompting and RAG cannot achieve. This approach minimizes cost and complexity by trying the simplest solutions first.

questions.question: A healthcare company needs a foundation model that understands medical terminology, can access the latest treatment guidelines, and responds in a formal clinical tone. Which combination of techniques is BEST?

options.A: Only prompt engineering
options.B: Continued pre-training on medical text for terminology, RAG with treatment guideline databases for current information, and fine-tuning for clinical tone and format
options.C: Only RAG with medical documents
options.D: Only fine-tuning on medical question-answer pairs

questions.explanation: This complex requirement is best addressed with a combination of all three techniques: (1) continued pre-training on medical text teaches the model medical terminology and concepts; (2) RAG with treatment guideline databases provides access to the latest guidelines without retraining; (3) fine-tuning on clinically-formatted examples teaches the model to respond in the required formal clinical tone. No single technique addresses all three requirements. Prompt engineering alone (A), RAG alone (C), or fine-tuning alone (D) each addresses only one aspect.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to choose fine-tuning over RAG?

options.A: You need the model to consistently adopt a specific writing style
options.B: You need the model to access information that is updated daily
options.C: You need the model to perform a specialized task format that prompting cannot achieve
options.D: You need the model to internalize domain-specific reasoning patterns

questions.explanation: Needing access to frequently updated information (B) is a reason to choose RAG, not fine-tuning. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model at training time, making it impossible to keep up with daily updates without daily retraining. RAG excels at providing current information by updating the knowledge base. The other options (A, C, D) are all valid reasons to choose fine-tuning: consistent style (A), specialized task formats (C), and internalized reasoning patterns (D) are all things that fine-tuning excels at.

questions.question: A company is evaluating their total cost of ownership for a foundation model solution. Which factors should they include in their cost analysis?

options.A: Only the per-token inference cost from the model provider
options.B: Inference costs, fine-tuning compute costs, RAG infrastructure costs (vector database, embedding, storage), data preparation labor, evaluation costs, and monitoring/operations overhead
options.C: Only the cost of the vector database
options.D: Only the salary of the prompt engineers

questions.explanation: A comprehensive total cost of ownership analysis for a foundation model solution must include all associated costs: inference costs (per-token or provisioned throughput), fine-tuning compute costs if applicable, RAG infrastructure costs (vector database hosting, embedding model calls, document storage), data preparation and curation labor, evaluation and testing costs, and ongoing monitoring and operations overhead. Looking at only one cost component (A, C, D) gives an incomplete picture and can lead to poor cost optimization decisions.
